raw_case_text: Early 2016, a male in his forties was admitted to a local hospital in Paramaribo, Suriname, because of muscle weakness in the legs and paresthesias in the hands and feet. He reported development of skin rash, red eyes, and arthralgia 7 days before the start of the paresthesias and muscle weakness. Physical examination upon admission showed symmetrical muscle weakness in the arms and legs; Medical Research Council (MRC) score 4 (ranging from 0; paralysis to 5; normal strength), absent deep tendon reflexes in the legs and decreased deep tendon reflexes in the arms. During admission, the patient developed a unilateral peripheral facial nerve paralysis and areflexia in both legs and arms. A lumbar puncture was performed 3 days after hospital admission, and an elevated protein level was found (1.98 g/L, N < 0.5 g/L) in the CSF in absence of cells. Due to the typical presentation of symmetrical flaccid muscle weakness with decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes, an albuminocytologic dissociation in the CSF and absence of a sensory level, fever, encephalopathy, or other clinical signs of myelum involvement, the diagnosis of GBS was considered the most probable. ZIKV real-time RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed locally on urine taken at day five after admission and was negative. A motor nerve conduction study (NCS) was performed 13 days after the start of muscle weakness. The NCS showed a decreased nerve conduction velocity (NCV) and compound muscle action potential (CMAP) and an increased distal motor latency (DML) (see Table S1 in Supplementary Material). The results of the NCS were consistent with the criteria for the primary demyelinating form of GBS according to the Hadden's criteria. A needle EMG was also performed and showed no abnormalities. The patient was still able to walk independently and, as symptoms remained relatively mild, was not treated with IVIg or PE. During admission, the muscle strength of the patient improved. He was discharged from the hospital after 11 days and followed-up at the neurology outpatient clinic until 12 weeks after hospital discharge, at which time he was fully recovered.

subjective.chief_complaint: A man in his forties presented in early 2016 with bilateral lower extremity muscle weakness and paresthesias of the hands and feet.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In early 2016, the patient was admitted to a hospital in Paramaribo, Suriname, with progressive muscle weakness in his legs and paresthesias in his hands and feet. Seven days prior to the onset of weakness and paresthesias, he had experienced an acute prodromal illness consisting of skin rash, red eyes (conjunctivitis), and arthralgia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Paramaribo, Suriname, presenting during the early 2016 Zika virus outbreak.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for leg weakness, hand and foot paresthesias, and preceding rash, red eyes, and arthralgia. Negative for fever or encephalopathy at admission.

objective.physical_examination: Admission neurological examination demonstrated symmetrical muscle weakness in the upper and lower extremities with a Medical Research Council (MRC) score of 4/5, absent deep tendon reflexes in the legs, and decreased deep tendon reflexes in the arms, without a sensory level, fever, encephalopathy, or signs of spinal cord involvement. During hospitalization, he developed a unilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy and complete areflexia in both arms and legs, though he remained able to walk independently.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture performed 3 days after admission revealed albuminocytologic dissociation with elevated CSF protein of 1.98 g/L (normal <0.5 g/L) and absence of cells. Motor nerve conduction study (NCS) performed 13 days after onset of weakness demonstrated decreased nerve conduction velocity (NCV), reduced compound muscle action potential (CMAP), and increased distal motor latency (DML) fulfilling Hadden's criteria for the primary demyelinating form of Guillain-Barre syndrome; needle electromyography (EMG) showed no abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary demyelinating Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS), Zika virus real-time RT-PCR negative. Urine tested locally by ZIKV qRT-PCR on hospital day 5 was negative. Because his symptoms remained relatively mild and he maintained independent ambulation, immunotherapy (intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange) was not administered. His muscle strength improved spontaneously during admission; he was discharged on hospital day 11 and achieved full recovery by 12 weeks of outpatient neurology follow-up.
